rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs. This leaves time for strongly retained compounds to elute during the final hold.
Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty and measure how the closest pairs respond to increased slope. The initial run has enough resolution margin to justify this acceleration.
Test temperature selectivity at the fast gradient, targeting the closely spaced central peaks. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.

Test an intermediate temperature to seek a selectivity window between the central co-elutions seen at 40 and 60 C. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature effects while retaining the zero time penalty.

Combine a modestly shallower gradient with an intermediate-high temperature to balance the two temperature-sensitive central separations. The estimated last-peak time remains below 8 minutes, potentially allowing full resolution without a time penalty.

Injection 5 already achieved the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a slightly shallower gradient to assess nearby selectivity and resolution margins while keeping the last peak near the zero-penalty time window.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a higher starting organic fraction for a nearby optimum with stronger resolution margins. This should shorten retention while revealing how the critical pairs respond to shifting the gradient window.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the limiting separation from injection 7 while preserving its favorable central-pair resolution. The last peak should remain below 8 minutes, offering another potential maximum-score method.

A slightly shallower slope should lift the limiting separation above 1.5 while retaining the other central pair's margin. Extrapolation from injections 7 and 8 places the last peak just below 8 minutes, potentially preserving the maximum CRF.

Test a higher starting fraction combined with a shallower slope to seek more balanced resolution margins around the maximum-score methods. The slope reduction should offset the loss in the earlier critical separation caused by raising phi0.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore the lower-temperature selectivity branch for an alternative fast, fully resolved method. Cooling may separate the central pair that nearly co-eluted at 40 C, while the short gradient limits the time penalty.

Explore a faster, high-temperature selectivity branch by shifting the gradient window and increasing its slope. These changes may move the central pair past its co-elution point at 60 C; injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction separates the limiting pair on the fast, high-temperature branch. A modestly longer gradient should protect neighboring separations while keeping retention well within the zero-time-penalty region.

Continue shifting the starting fraction upward to improve the limiting high-temperature separation, with a longer gradient to preserve neighboring resolution. Monitor the first two peaks closely because their retention and separation are decreasing.

Return to the proven 55 C region and slightly flatten injection 8's gradient to lift its limiting resolution above 1.5. This should provide another maximum-score method with balanced critical-pair margins and a last-peak time near 8 minutes.

Trim the gradient endpoint while preserving injection 5's successful slope and starting composition. Its last peak left at approximately 0.57 organic fraction, so all peaks should remain within this shorter gradient and retain the maximum CRF.

Test a slope between injections 8 and 15 to seek full resolution with a slightly shorter elution time than injection 15. The trimmed endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window, and both critical resolutions are predicted to exceed 1.5.

Assess the temperature sensitivity of injection 17's maximum-score method by lowering only T by 5 C. This isolates whether its critical-pair margins survive cooling and helps define the operating window around the optimum.

Complete the temperature bracket around injection 17 by testing 60 C with the same gradient. This will establish the upper-temperature selectivity boundary while the previously achieved maximum CRF remains secured.

Refine near the proven optimum with a slope just shallower than injection 6, testing the lower-slope boundary for full central-pair resolution. All peaks should remain inside the gradient, with the last peak near 8 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 10 to improve its limiting separation while retaining the stronger margin of the other central pair. This tests whether a higher-starting-organic method can also reach the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 21 to push its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the other central pair's margin. The last peak is estimated near 9 minutes, testing the edge of the zero-time-penalty window.

Refine around injection 15 with a slightly shallower gradient to increase the earlier critical-pair separation. The later critical pair should remain above 1.5, and the predicted last-peak time remains below the observed 9-minute zero-penalty boundary.

Trim injection 15's endpoint while preserving its starting fraction and gradient slope. The last peak previously eluted near 0.56 organic fraction, so this shorter programmed gradient should retain full separation and the maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to refine between the successful slopes of injections 15 and 23, with all peaks expected inside the gradient. Both critical resolutions should remain above 1.5 with no time penalty; injection 5 already secures the maximum achievable CRF.
